data.title: Initial Level Placement
data.description: A high-level scan to establish your current CEFR baseline (A2-B2).

sections.sentence: Choose the correct action in progress.
sections.explain: Use the past continuous for an action that was already in progress when another past action happened.

words.word: When I arrived, they were eating dinner.
When I arrived, they eat dinner.
When I arrived, they have eaten dinner.

sections.explain: 'Much' is normally used with uncountable nouns such as 'time'.

words.word: We do not have many time before the train leaves.
We do not have much time before the train leaves.
We do not have a few time before the train leaves.

sections.summary: A2: Present Continuous for Future Plans.
sections.explain: The present continuous can describe a fixed future arrangement.

words.word: I meet the dentist at ten tomorrow.
I am meet the dentist at ten tomorrow.
I am meeting the dentist at ten tomorrow.

sections.sentence: Choose the correct tense for a finished time.
sections.summary: B1: Past Simple and Present Perfect.
sections.explain: Use the past simple with a finished time expression such as 'last year'.

words.word: I have visited Rome last year.
I visited Rome last year.
I have been visiting Rome last year.

sections.explain: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person.

words.word: The woman which helped me was very kind.
The woman whose helped me was very kind.
The woman who helped me was very kind.

sections.sentence: Choose the sentence with the correct condition.
sections.explain: 'Unless' means 'if not', so it is followed by an affirmative verb form.

words.word: We will miss the bus unless we leave now.
We will miss the bus unless we do not leave now.
We would miss the bus unless we will leave now.

sections.sentence: Choose the best deduction about the past.
sections.explain: 'Must have' expresses a strong logical deduction about a completed past event.

words.word: The lights are off, so they must leave already.
The lights are off, so they must have left already.
The lights are off, so they must be left already.

sections.explain: A past condition can have a present result: 'If + past perfect' followed by 'would + base verb'.

words.word: If I accepted that job, I would have lived in Paris now.
If I had accepted that job, I would have lived in Paris then.
If I had accepted that job, I would live in Paris now.

sections.explain: A past participle clause can replace a passive relative clause when both clauses have the same subject.

words.word: Built in the eighteenth century, the house requires extensive repairs.
Building in the eighteenth century, the house requires extensive repairs.
Having build in the eighteenth century, the house requires extensive repairs.

sections.explain: When 'Not until' begins the sentence, the main clause requires auxiliary inversion.

words.word: Not until the meeting ended we understood the problem.
Not until did the meeting end we understood the problem.
Not until the meeting ended did we understand the problem.
